authority.scope: Exactly13 held architecture/network acronym cards;10 prior draft revalidations,2 bounded scope/protection revisions,1 unchanged clear chip meaning with identity hold. LOCAL only.

rows.currentMeaning: Security model based on never trust, always verify with continuous checks for users, devices, and sessions.

replacement.meaning: Architecture that protects resources through explicit authentication and authorization, without granting implicit trust solely because of network location or device ownership.

rows.rootCause: HOLD: never-trust/always-verify plus continuous checks does not state resource access authorization or removal of implicit trust based on network location/ownership.
rows.protectionBoundary: Authentication alone does not grant access to every resource.

sourceReferences.claimScope: Abstract: resource focus, no location/ownership-only implicit trust, distinct authentication/authorization.

rows.expansion: Bring Your Own Device / Corporate-Owned Personally Enabled / Choose Your Own Device
rows.currentMeaning: Mobile-device ownership models with different security and privacy tradeoffs.

replacement.meaning: BYOD uses personally owned devices for work. COPE uses organization-owned devices with permitted personal use. CYOD offers an approved device list; ownership and funding depend on the organization's policy.

rows.rootCause: HOLD: the meaning only announces different security/privacy tradeoffs; it does not distinguish personally owned work devices, corporate-owned personally enabled devices, or selection from an approved device catalogue.
rows.protectionBoundary: Selection from an approved list does not settle ownership or funding.

sourceReferences.claimScope: Earlier bound section5.1.3 CYOD evidence retained; final landing page reread, fresh PDF retrieval unavailable. No full mobile-policy audit.

rows.expansion: Infrastructure / Platform / Software as a Service
rows.currentMeaning: Cloud service models with different responsibility split between customer and provider.

replacement.meaning: IaaS provides processing, storage and networking while customers control their operating systems and applications. PaaS provides a managed platform for customer-deployed applications. SaaS provides provider-run applications. Customer access, data and configuration responsibilities still depend on the service and agreement.

rows.rootCause: HOLD: different responsibility split supplies no individual service capability or customer/provider control boundary for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
rows.protectionBoundary: A provider-run application does not eliminate customer access/data/configuration duties.

sourceReferences.claimScope: Section2 service/deployment definitions; bounded capability/control distinctions, not modern service conformance.

rows.currentMeaning: Unique hardware address assigned to a network interface.

replacement.meaning: Address used by a network interface at the link layer. It may be assigned locally or randomized, so it is not reliable proof of a unique physical device. Here MAC refers to media access control.

rows.rootCause: HOLD: calling every MAC a unique hardware address overstates permanent physical-device identity; the existing support identity also collides with Mandatory Access Control.
rows.protectionBoundary: An interface can use a locally assigned or randomized address.

sourceReferences.claimScope: Private/rotating Wi-Fi MAC addresses as a counterexample to fixed hardware identity; no device configuration performed.

rows.currentMeaning: Systems used to monitor or control physical industrial processes.

replacement.meaning: OT comprises programmable systems or devices that monitor or control physical devices, processes or events. Industrial control systems are one type of OT; building automation, transport and physical access systems are other examples.

rows.rootCause: HOLD: the single industrial-process meaning does not distinguish broader operational technology from industrial control systems.
rows.protectionBoundary: Building automation is an OT example beyond industrial processes.

sourceReferences.scope: Final2023 abstract: OT programmable systems/devices interacting with physical environments; examples include ICS, building automation, transport and physical access. New draft is reviewer synthesis, not a current system security assessment.

rows.expansion: Software Development Life Cycle / Software Development Life-Cycle Methodology
rows.currentMeaning: Structured process for planning, building, testing, and maintaining software securely.

replacement.meaning: Planning, building, testing and maintaining software follow a development life cycle. Security practices need explicit integration into that work; a lifecycle or methodology label alone does not establish secure software.

rows.rootCause: HOLD: the shared process meaning does not distinguish a development lifecycle from a lifecycle methodology and implies security without explicit secure-development practices.
rows.protectionBoundary: A named lifecycle or methodology does not establish integrated secure practices.

sourceReferences.scope: Final2022 SSDF1.1 abstract: secure practices usually need explicit integration into SDLC models. Does not establish a universal SDLM expansion or methodology taxonomy; grouping hold remains.

rows.currentMeaning: Chip that combines many computer components into one integrated circuit.
rows.rootCause: HOLD SUPPORT IDENTITY ONLY: the chip definition is clear, but its existing sy0701.term.soc support node also represents Security Operations Center.
rows.protectionBoundary: Clear chip wording does not disambiguate a shared support node.

rows.currentMeaning: Adds encryption and integrity protection to real-time voice or video traffic.

replacement.meaning: An RTP security extension supporting confidentiality, message authentication and replay protection. Actual protections depend on the selected profile, transforms, keys and configuration; null encryption does not hide media.

rows.rootCause: HOLD: the delivered definition asserts encryption and integrity without identifying a profile or enabled protections; the whole card leaves an unconditional guarantee ambiguous.
rows.protectionBoundary: A stipulated null-encryption transform does not hide media.

sourceReferences.claimScope: Historical SRTP sections4.1.3,9.5: null encryption and weak/null SRTP authentication distinctions; not a current algorithm recommendation.

rows.currentMeaning: Encrypted remote administration protocol, commonly used for command-line access.

replacement.meaning: Protocol commonly used for remote command-line administration over a transport with negotiated encryption and integrity protection. Confidentiality depends on the encryption actually in use; the historical none cipher provides none.

rows.rootCause: HOLD: encrypted remote administration describes the intended common SSH use, but the unqualified delivered sentence leaves negotiated confidentiality as a categorical property.
rows.protectionBoundary: The historical none cipher is not confidentiality or a recommended configuration.

sourceReferences.claimScope: Historical section6.3 none option supplies no encryption and is not recommended; no assertion about installed clients.

rows.currentMeaning: Encrypted tunnel that protects traffic across an untrusted network.

replacement.meaning: A logical private network carried over shared infrastructure. Secure remote-access or site-to-site VPNs commonly use encrypted tunnels, but the generic VPN label alone does not guarantee encryption.

rows.rootCause: HOLD: a generic VPN is defined as an encrypted protective tunnel, omitting legitimate VPN architectures without cryptographic privacy and the necessary secure-tunnel scope.
rows.protectionBoundary: The cited BGP/MPLS architecture lacks cryptographic privacy.

sourceReferences.claimScope: Sections1.2 and6.5 distinguish shared VPN infrastructure and optional encryption; not a deployment security assessment.

rows.currentMeaning: Forged wireless management frames force clients to disconnect from Wi-Fi.
rows.currentExample: Fake deauth frames kick a laptop off corporate Wi-Fi so it reconnects to an evil twin.

replacement.meaning: In this attack context, forged deauthentication or disassociation frames attempt to terminate a Wi-Fi connection. These frames also have legitimate uses; negotiated management-frame protection can reject forgeries.
replacement.example: A client without negotiated protected management frames accepts forged deauthentication frames and disconnects. This alone does not establish that it joins an evil twin.

rows.rootCause: The bare term and combined disassociation/deauthentication expansion are defined only as forged frames forcing disconnects. Legitimate protocol transitions are conflated with attack traffic, and frame acceptance/protection is left unconditional.
rows.protectionBoundary: Protected management frames can reject forgeries; a disconnect does not establish evil-twin association.

sourceReferences.claimScope: Implementation-specific PMF description protects deauthentication/disassociation frames; no universal attack-prevention guarantee.

rows.currentMeaning: Attacker secretly intercepts or changes communication between two parties.
rows.currentExample: A coffee-shop Wi-Fi attacker reads unencrypted login traffic between a laptop and website.

replacement.example: A malicious Wi-Fi gateway forwards traffic between a laptop and a website while reading the unencrypted login data passing through it.

rows.rootCause: The label requires an intervening communication position, but the coffee-shop example only supplies reading plaintext traffic. A passive receiver can read exposed wireless traffic without relaying or mediating it.
rows.protectionBoundary: A passive plaintext listener need not be a forwarding intermediary.

sourceReferences.claimScope: Section3.5 distinguishes attacker position from mere passive reading; gateway example is an explicit reviewer construction.

rows.currentMeaning: Copies contactless identifiers to bypass physical access controls.
rows.currentExample: A hidden scanner copies an employee badge on the subway for later building access.

replacement.meaning: Replicating a contactless credential or its data to impersonate it. Copying a readable identifier bypasses access checks only where the reader relies on that identifier without effective additional authentication.
replacement.example: A badge system authorizes entry using only a readable static identifier. A copied identifier presented by an emulator is accepted because the reader performs no additional credential authentication.

rows.rootCause: The combined label reduces contactless credential cloning to identifier copying and implies an access bypass without identifying a vulnerable credential/reader policy. Its subway scanning illustration supplies no tag, range or authentication context.
rows.protectionBoundary: A readable identifier alone does not satisfy effective additional credential authentication.

sourceReferences.claimScope: UID-only authorization versus added credential authentication in a scoped EV-charging example; badge case is a reviewer analogy, not a universal contactless exploit.
